analysis.one_liner: Bans lobbyists-turned-officials, forces officials to divest stocks, strengthens anti-corruption enforcement, and expands campaign finance rules.
analysis.headline: Warren's anti-corruption and ethics bill, introduced in the Senate's final days with no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the ethics rules for everyone in and around the federal government. It would have banned former lobbyists — especially corporate lobbyists — from taking government jobs for years, required senior officials and members of Congress to sell off individual stocks and other conflicted investments, banned 'golden parachute' payments from private employers, and blocked companies from hiring officials they had recently lobbied. It also would have created a new Office of Public Integrity to enforce ethics rules, imposed a code of conduct on the Supreme Court, banned corporate PAC money, expanded public financing of elections, and made lobbying, political intelligence, and online political advertising far more transparent. It was introduced in the last two weeks of the congressional session, never received a hearing, and died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who currently bear the cost of decisions made by officials with personal financial stakes and by former officials rotating through lobbying firms. The bill would also benefit government agencies and ethics watchdogs, which would gain real enforcement tools, and would reduce the influence of lobbying firms, large banks, and corporate PAC money over lawmaking.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens and ethics oversight bodies

how_it_helps.text: It bars former lobbyists — and for six years, former corporate lobbyists — from taking jobs at executive agencies or congressional offices, tightening the revolving door between industry and government.

It requires senior government officials, including Members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President, to divest financial interests that pose conflicts of interest, and bans officials from trading securities affected by their official actions.

It bans 'golden parachutes' — bonus and severance payments from private employers to officials leaving for government service — and extends restrictions on former officials going to work for giant banks, big contractors, and companies they regulated, with civil penalties of 1-5% of a violator's annual net profit.

It creates an Office of Public Integrity to enforce ethics and lobbying laws, expands the Office of Congressional Ethics, establishes a code of conduct and complaint process for Supreme Court justices, and bars corporate PAC contributions and donations to members from companies under their committees' jurisdiction.

It expands public financing of Senate and presidential campaigns around small-dollar contributions, bans corporate fundraising by members, and requires online political ads to carry disclaimers and disclosure.

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms and corporate lobbying operations, large banks and government contractors that hire former officials, and senior government officials and members of Congress, who would have to divest individual stocks and accept limits on post-government employment. Incumbents also lose corporate PAC money and face stricter disclosure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lobbyists, big banks, and incumbent officials

drawbacks.text: The bill would require senior government officials and Members of Congress to divest individual stocks and securities, restricting their ability to invest like other citizens, and would establish new federal investment accounts to absorb divested assets, a large administrative undertaking.

The bill's sweeping ethics, lobbying, and rulemaking provisions (including a progressive tax on lobbying expenditures and broad new enforcement machinery in a new Office of Public Integrity) would be difficult and costly to administer, and critics could reasonably argue some rules, such as long cooling-off periods before hiring former officials, could push expertise out of government rather than into it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public upside would have been meaningful but indirect: the bill targets how officials may profit from office rather than any pocketbook issue directly. The costs are real and acknowledged by its own design: it would bar senior officials from owning individual securities, which would force asset sales and complicate recruiting for top jobs, and the blanket corporate-lobbyist hiring ban and broad anti-lobbying rules would restrict the career movement of experienced professionals in both directions. Those are legitimate tradeoffs, not fatal flaws, but the bill was never debated or amended, so Congress never weighed them in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate's final days and referred to the Finance Committee, where it sat without a hearing, cosponsor, or vote until the Congress ended and the bill expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 20, 2022 — two weeks before the 117th Congress ended — and read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, including from either party.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote. The bill died in committee when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms, large banks, and incumbent officials who would have faced divestment and hiring bans keep the current rules; the public keeps the revolving-door and conflict-of-interest rules as they were.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the Senate, where it was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action: no hearing, no markup, no report before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other senator cosponsored, so the bill's level of support inside either party was never measured — the only recorded actions are Warren's introduction and the committee referral.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and corporate lobbying arms
industries.note: The bill bans former corporate lobbyists from government service for six years, taxes lobbying expenditures progressively, bans contingent-fee lobbying, and imposes new disclosure and enforcement requirements under a new Office of Public Integrity.

Companies above $150 billion in market cap or receiving over $5 billion in federal contract revenue would be barred from hiring senior officials for four years after they leave government, facing civil penalties of 1-5% of annual net profit for violations.

industries.industry: Corporate PACs and large political donors
industries.note: The bill bans corporate PAC contributions, prohibits corporations from fundraising for members, lowers contribution limits, and creates public small-dollar financing for Senate and presidential campaigns, reducing the value of concentrated political money.

industries.industry: Political intelligence and online political advertising
industries.note: The bill requires political intelligence firms to register under lobbying law, bans post-government officials from selling policy information to securities markets, and extends disclosure and disclaimer rules to online political ads and platforms.
